entries.title: Skin to skin and the first feeds
entries.body: Many parents find that holding a newborn skin to skin helps the baby settle, and either of you can do it. The first milk, colostrum, comes in small amounts, and frequent feeds matter more than long ones in these first days. Some early weight loss is common. Tell your pediatrician or a lactation consultant if you are unsure how feeding is going.

entries.title: Reading your baby's hunger cues
entries.body: Early hunger cues for babies under 6 months include hands to mouth, turning toward the breast or bottle, lip smacking, and clenched hands. Crying tends to come late, so the earlier signs are easier to answer. A full baby often closes the mouth, turns away, or relaxes the hands. Take turns feeding so you both learn your baby's own signals.

entries.title: How often a newborn eats
entries.body: Newborns have tiny stomachs and may want to eat every 1 to 3 hours in the first days, and formula-fed babies also feed 8 to 12 times in 24 hours at first. Cluster feeding is common. Ask your pediatrician whether your baby needs vitamin D drops, and call if you are worried about how much your baby is taking.

entries.title: Newborn and hearing screening
entries.body: Newborn screening is a state program that tests a few drops of heel blood for serious conditions so treatment can start early if needed. Hearing screening, ideally by 1 month of age, is a quick, painless check. If a result needs a follow-up, your pediatrician can explain the next step. Keep the paperwork where both of you can find it.

entries.title: Setting up a safe sleep space
entries.body: Place your baby on their back for every nap and night until age 1, on a firm, flat surface with only a fitted sheet. Keep the baby's own sleep space in your room, not in your bed, for at least the first 6 months. At 1 month babies mostly eat, sleep, and cry. Keep pillows, bumpers, and soft toys out of the crib.

entries.title: When the crying gets hard
entries.body: Daily crying often peaks around 6 weeks and usually eases by 3 to 4 months. Long, hard-to-soothe crying is normal, but shaking, throwing, or hitting a baby is never the right response. If you feel yourself getting angry, lay the baby down safely, step away, and check back every 5 to 10 minutes, or hand the baby to your partner or a friend.

entries.title: Your own mood matters too
entries.body: Baby blues are mild mood changes and tiredness many mothers feel in the first 2 weeks. Stronger or longer-lasting symptoms, which most often begin 4 to 8 weeks after birth, are worth raising with a professional. About one in ten dads also experiences postpartum depression. Check in with each other this week, and tell your doctor if either of you feels unusually low.

entries.title: First real smiles
entries.body: Real smiles often appear around 6 weeks, and smiling back when you talk or smile at them is something many babies do by 2 months. Babies focus best on faces about 8 to 12 inches away, so hold yours close and talk slowly, then pause to see if your baby answers. Babies vary, so bring any questions to the check-up around 2 months.

entries.title: A little tummy time each day
entries.body: Start tummy time soon after coming home and build toward about 15 to 30 minutes in total each day by around 7 weeks, in short sessions while the baby is awake and watched. Lifting the head on the tummy is a milestone many babies reach by 2 months. If your baby protests, lie back and put the baby on your chest. Sleep is always on the back.

entries.title: Startles and early reflexes
entries.body: Many early movements are reflexes. The startle reflex usually peaks in the first month and fades around 2 months, so you may see it softening now. Rooting and sucking help newborns find food in the first weeks. As reflexes fade, bringing hands to the mouth and pushing up on the forearms are milestones many babies reach by 4 months. Mention to your pediatrician any clear difference between your baby's two sides.

entries.title: Cooing and talking back
entries.body: Around 2 months, babies often start cooing and repeating vowel sounds, and these early exchanges teach turn-taking. Babies tend to like the human voice, especially higher pitches. Talk during diaper changes and feeds, leave a pause, and answer the sounds you get. Making sounds back when you talk is a milestone many babies show by 4 months.

entries.title: Fussy evenings and what helps
entries.body: Rocking, walking with the baby in a carrier, white noise, and swaddling can all soothe a fussy baby. Space feeds at least 2 to 2 and a half hours apart to avoid overfeeding. Colic usually eases by 3 to 4 months. Trade shifts so each of you gets a real break. Ask your pediatrician if the crying seems different from usual.

entries.title: Car seat basics
entries.body: Use a rear-facing car seat with a harness from birth until about age 2 to 4, and keep your child rear-facing until they reach the seat's weight or height limit. Never put a rear-facing seat in the front seat because of airbags. Practice the installation together, read the seat's manual, and ask your pediatrician where to get the fit checked. Your baby is heading toward the 4-month milestones.

entries.title: Sleep changes around 3 months
entries.body: Stop swaddling once a baby begins to roll, usually around 3 months. Regular sleep cycles develop only gradually, around 4 months, so keep nights low-key with dim light and little chatter at feeds. Many parents keep days lively for contrast. Always place your baby on their back for every sleep, naps included.

entries.title: Floor play builds strong muscles
entries.body: Movements often get smoother around 3 months, with relaxed hands, stronger kicks, and more purposeful grasping. Bouncer seats and harnesses limit the muscle practice babies need, so floor time on a blanket helps. Swinging at toys is a milestone many babies reach by 4 months, so hold a toy within reach. Mention it if your baby seems very limp or does not use one side.

entries.title: Sharing a first book
entries.body: Read with your baby from birth, since babies soak up the rhythm and sounds of speech. Younger babies enjoy your voice, eye contact, and simple rhymes. If your baby looks away or fusses, take a break, because you do not need to finish the book. A short story before naps or bedtime can become a calming cue, and each parent can pick a favorite.

entries.title: Sharing the nights and the days
entries.body: Share the night work, such as diaper changes and nighttime shifts, to reduce sleep deprivation. Responding to crying builds trust, and babies can bond closely with several people. Pick one stretch this week where one of you takes the baby while the other sleeps, then swap. Looking for your attention is a milestone many babies reach by 4 months.

entries.title: Babbling and chuckles begin
entries.body: Around 4 months, babies start babbling with the rhythms of their home language, and repeating the sounds back encourages it. Many babies also chuckle when you try to make them laugh and smile on purpose to get your attention. Try a game of silly faces and sounds. Bring any questions to the check-up around 4 months.

entries.title: Rolling over, tummy to back
entries.body: Rolling from tummy to back is a milestone many babies reach heading toward 6 months. That direction usually comes first, and most babies roll both ways by about 7 months. Rolling can start suddenly, so never leave your baby alone on a bed, sofa, or changing table. The floor is the safest place for play. Timing varies, so ask your pediatrician if you wonder.

entries.title: Everything goes in the mouth
entries.body: Putting things in the mouth to explore them is common around 6 months, and mouthing books is a good sign of interest, with sturdy board books holding up best. Check the floor for small objects that could cause choking, and keep button batteries out of reach. Agree on a quick floor sweep you each do before play.

entries.title: Settling to sleep
entries.body: From 4 months on, putting babies down drowsy rather than fully asleep can help them learn to fall asleep on their own. Waking and settling again within a few minutes is normal around 6 months. Still respond to hunger or illness, and keep placing your baby on the back to sleep. Pick a simple bedtime routine you can both repeat.

entries.title: Faces, mirrors, familiar people
entries.body: Recognizing familiar people, liking to look in a mirror, and laughing are common around 6 months. Hold your baby up to a mirror and make faces together. Babies can form close bonds with several people, so partners, grandparents, and sitters can all have a place. Give each adult some regular one-on-one time with the baby.

entries.title: Signs of readiness for solids
entries.body: Solid foods can begin around 6 months and should not start before 4 months. Signs of readiness include sitting up with or without support, controlling the head and neck, opening the mouth for food, and swallowing food instead of pushing it out. Watch for these signs together rather than counting days, and ask your pediatrician what fits your baby.

entries.title: Practicing to sit
entries.body: Babies need support while they practice sitting, leaning forward on their arms at first, and by about 6 to 8 months many stay upright without help. Leaning on hands when sitting and pushing up on straight arms during tummy time are common now. Sit on the floor with cushions around your baby and offer toys at chest height.

entries.title: Starting solids, slowly
entries.body: Offer one single-ingredient food at a time, wait 3 to 5 days between new foods so reactions are easy to spot, and start with smooth, mashed, or pureed textures. Closing the lips to show no more is a sign of fullness, so let your baby decide when a meal is over. If your baby has severe eczema or an egg allergy, ask your pediatrician about when to introduce peanut.

entries.title: Your baby's first teeth
entries.body: Baby teeth usually appear between 6 and 10 months, with fussiness, drooling, and chewing on things among the common signs. A chilled teether, a cool damp washcloth, or a clean finger rubbed on the gums can help. Fever and diarrhea are not teething symptoms, so call your pediatrician if you see them. Ask before using any pain medicine.

entries.title: Foods to hold back for now
entries.body: Avoid honey before 12 months because of the risk of botulism, and hold off on cow's milk as a drink and on juice until after the first birthday. Also avoid added sugars and high-salt foods for babies. Read labels together, and share the list with every caregiver so the rules stay the same.

entries.title: Babyproofing before crawling
entries.body: Secure hazards as soon as a child starts to crawl or walk: store cleaning products and medicines out of reach and sight, ideally in locked cabinets, and check floors for small objects and button batteries. Poison Help is 1-800-222-1222. Tour each room at baby's eye level together, then save the number in both phones. Sitting and moving objects hand to hand are common by 9 months.

entries.title: Taking turns with sounds
entries.body: Making many different babbling sounds, such as mamamama, is common around 9 months. Babies may stumble onto words like mama before using them on purpose, and conversation is two-way, so ask a question and wait for a reply. Narrate your day out loud. If you wonder about your baby's sounds, mention it at the next check-up.

entries.title: Preparing food to prevent choking
entries.body: Babies can choke as they learn to chew and swallow. Cut round foods like grapes and cherry tomatoes, skip whole nuts, popcorn, and hard raw produce, and seat your baby upright in a high chair, never eating while crawling, walking, or riding in a car. Watch closely at every meal. Ask your pediatrician what to do if a child chokes.

entries.title: Sitting and rolling both ways
entries.body: By about 7 months babies often roll both ways, sit with and then without hand support, bear weight on their legs, and pass toys between hands. Offer toys just out of reach to encourage moving. Call your pediatrician if your baby seems very stiff or floppy, reaches with only one hand, or does not bear weight on the legs.

entries.title: Responding to name and no
entries.body: Around 7 months babies respond to their name, start reacting to the word no, and read feelings from your tone of voice. Turning when called by name is a milestone many babies reach by 9 months. Use a calm, steady voice for limits and a warm one for play. Call your baby's name from across the room and see who gets the first turn.

entries.title: Anchoring furniture and gating stairs
entries.body: A child goes to the emergency department for a furniture or TV tip-over about once an hour, and anti-tip anchors cost about $5 to $25 and take minutes to install. Put heavy items low, never place a TV on a dresser, and mount stair gates to wall studs rather than using accordion-style gates. Many babies this age bear weight on their legs, so mobility is close.

entries.title: Bath time and water safety
entries.body: Infants can drown in 1 or 2 inches of water within seconds, so keep a hand on your baby in the bath and never leave a baby alone or with another young child near water. Bath seats can tip. Check bath water with your wrist or elbow, latch toilet lids, and keep the bathroom door closed. Agree who is on bath duty, and consider learning infant CPR together.

entries.title: Crawling, scooting, or something else
entries.body: Crawling is usually mastered between 7 and 10 months, and some babies scoot or slither instead, which is fine if they use both sides of the body equally. Getting into a sitting position alone is a milestone many babies reach by 9 months. Clear a safe floor space and get down to baby's level. Tell your pediatrician if your baby is not sitting alone by 9 months.

entries.title: Why strangers feel scary now
entries.body: Stranger anxiety is an early emotional milestone: a baby who was calm with new people may now tense up or cry, even with relatives. Shyness, clinginess, or fear around strangers are common by 9 months. This reflects a new ability to tell familiar from unfamiliar, not poor parenting. Hold your baby while visitors say hello and let the baby warm up.

entries.title: Peekaboo and hidden toys
entries.body: Smiling or laughing during peekaboo and looking for objects dropped out of sight are milestones many babies reach by 9 months. Mirror games, such as naming body parts or playing peekaboo with reflections, are fun too. Drop a toy and let your baby look for it, or hide one under a cloth while your baby watches. Take turns hiding so both of you get to play.

entries.title: Finger foods and the pincer grasp
entries.body: Raking food toward themselves with the fingers is a milestone many babies reach by 9 months, and the pincer grasp, using index finger and thumb, usually develops around 9 months. Offer soft food that dissolves easily or is cooked until easy to mash, in small pieces, and stay close. Go over the choking risks together. Messy meals are part of learning.

entries.title: Separation anxiety and goodbyes
entries.body: Separation anxiety often peaks around 9 months, because babies do not yet understand time and even short absences can upset them. Short, predictable goodbyes work better than lingering, and coming back when you said you would builds trust. Practice brief separations at home, and let both parents take turns with drop-offs. Reacting when a caregiver leaves is common at this age.

entries.title: Looking at the 9-month mark
entries.body: Sitting without support, passing objects from hand to hand, and looking for dropped objects are milestones many babies reach by 9 months. Tell the pediatrician if your baby is not sitting alone by then. Many families have a check-up around now, so each of you can jot down what you have noticed, including new sounds and moves. Babies develop at their own pace.

entries.title: Pulling up and cruising
entries.body: Pulling up to stand and walking while holding onto furniture are milestones many babies reach by 1 year. Babies pull up, cruise along furniture, and often take first steps around the first birthday. Make sure furniture is anchored and low shelves are safe to grab. Stand a short distance away with a toy and let your baby come to you.

entries.title: Why to skip the walker
entries.body: Do not use baby walkers. Babies in walkers can roll down stairs, reach hot items, and move more than 3 feet in a second, so injuries happen even with an adult watching. Walkers do not help children walk. Stationary activity centers, play yards, and floor time are safer, and pulling up to stand is a milestone many babies reach by 1 year.

entries.title: Waving, pointing, and gestures
entries.body: Waving goodbye and pausing or stopping when told no are milestones many babies reach by 1 year. Babies often point or gesture at what they want while words are still on the way. When your baby points, name the thing and wait for a reaction. Wave goodbye together at every departure, so both of you can practice with your baby.

entries.title: Learning to drink from a cup
entries.body: Drinking from an open cup while you hold it is a milestone many babies reach by 1 year. Let your baby practice at meals with you holding the cup. Juice is not recommended before 12 months, and cow's milk as a drink waits until after the first birthday. Ask your pediatrician what to put in the cup.

entries.title: Board books and pointing
entries.body: Babies of 6 to 11 months enjoy sturdy board books, textures, naming pictures, and repetition, and mouthing books is normal. By 12 to 24 months many toddlers point to named pictures. Read the same favorite again and ask where something is. Playing back-and-forth games is a milestone many babies reach by 1 year, and a book can be one.

entries.title: First words in any form
entries.body: Any consistent sound a baby uses for a person or object counts as a word. Some babies have two or three words by age 1, and many still babble with the rhythm of speech at 12 months. Calling a parent by a special name is a milestone many babies reach by 1 year. Use the same names for things and mention any questions about speech at the check-up.

entries.title: Containers, blocks, and play
entries.body: Putting objects inside containers and searching for hidden objects are milestones many babies reach by 1 year. Banging blocks together and putting things in and taking them out are great play too. Offer a plastic bowl and large safe objects, nothing small enough to fit in the mouth. Hide a toy under a cup and let your baby find it.

entries.title: Fears and strong opinions
entries.body: Babies of this age may refuse certain foods, resist hearing no, and become afraid of things like the dark, thunder, or vacuum cleaners. Removing the source when you can, using a night-light, and staying calm and reassuring can help. Pausing when told no is a milestone many babies reach by 1 year. Agree between you how you each respond.

entries.title: Night wakings near the first birthday
entries.body: Waking and settling again is a normal part of baby sleep, and you still respond to needs such as hunger, a wet diaper, or illness. Keep placing your baby on their back to sleep until age 1. If nights are rough, trade off so each of you gets a longer stretch. Ask your pediatrician about any sleep worry.

entries.title: Looking after yourselves too
entries.body: About one in ten dads experiences postpartum depression, and anxiety can appear in pregnancy or the first postpartum year. These conditions are treatable, and perinatal depression can affect any pregnant or postpartum woman. Check in with each other this week, and tell your doctor if either of you has felt low or anxious for a while.

entries.title: Shoes and first steps
entries.body: Babies often take first steps around their first birthday, and shoes are needed only once a baby walks outside: closed-toe, flexible, with nonskid soles and room to grow. Check the fit monthly, since feet grow quickly. Special inserts or arch supports are not needed. Walking while holding onto furniture is common by 1 year.

entries.title: Moving from formula and baby foods
entries.body: Toddlers can gradually switch from formula to plain, unsweetened, pasteurized whole cow's milk or fortified unsweetened dairy alternatives after the first birthday, such as by replacing one formula feeding at a time. Also avoid added sugars, and juice before 12 months. Talk with your pediatrician about amounts and timing before you change.

entries.title: Around the first birthday
entries.body: Waving, calling a parent by a special name, and pulling up to stand are milestones many babies reach by 1 year. Bring up with your pediatrician if your baby is not crawling, not standing with support, not searching for hidden items, not saying single words, or not pointing. Write down questions together before the 12-month check-up. Babies grow at their own pace.
